danish.title: Første epilog (1813–20) — Kapitel 5
paragraphs: Natasjas (Natasja Rostova) bryllup med Bezukhov (Pierre), der fandt sted i 1813, var den sidste lykkelige begivenhed i den gamle Rostov-families liv. Grev Ilja Rostov døde samme år, og som det altid sker, opløstes familiegruppen efter faderens død.

Det forgående års begivenheder: Moskvas brand og flugten derfra, fyrst Andrej Bolkonskijs død, Natasjas fortvivlelse, Petjas (Petja Rostov) død og den gamle grevindes sorg faldt slag efter slag over den gamle grevens hoved. Han syntes ude af stand til at forstå meningen med alle disse begivenheder og bøjede sit gamle hoved, som ventede han og indbød nye og knusende slag. Snart virkede han bange og forvirret, snart unaturligt livlig og foretagsom.

Forberedelserne til Natasjas bryllup optog ham en tid. Han bestilte middage og souper og forsøgte åbenbart at virke munter, men hans munterhed var ikke smitsom, som den plejede at være; tværtimod vakte den medlidenhed hos dem, der kendte og holdt af ham.

Da Pierre og hans kone var rejst, blev han meget stille og begyndte at klage over nedstemthed. Få dage senere blev han syg og gik til sengs. Han indså fra begyndelsen, at han ikke ville rejse sig igen, trods lægens opmuntring. Grevinden sad en fjorten dage i en lænestol ved hans hovedpude uden at klæde sig af. Hver gang hun gav ham sin medicin, hulkede han stille og kyssede hendes hånd. På sin sidste dag bad han grædende hende og sin fraværende søn om tilgivelse for at have sat familiens formue over styr — det, han betragtede som sin hovedskyld. Efter at have modtaget nadveren og de sidste salver døde han stille; og næste dag fyldte en skare af bekendte, der kom for at vise den afdøde den sidste ære, det lejede hus. Alle disse bekendte, der så mange gange havde spist og danset til hans levende musik og så mange gange havde grint af ham, sagde nu alle med en samstemmig følelse af indre bebrejdelse og bevægelse, som for at retfærdiggøre sig selv: »Nå, hvad man end kan sige, var han en sjælden fin mand. Man finder ikke den slags nu om dage... Og hvem har ikke sine svagheder?«
Det var netop, da grevens affærer var blevet så indviklede, at det var umuligt at sige, hvad der ville ske, hvis han levede et år til, at han uventet døde.

Nikolaj var med den russiske hær i Paris, da nyheden om hans fars død nåede ham. Han indgav straks sin afskedsbegæring, og uden at vente på, at den blev godkendt, tog han orlov og rejste til Moskva. Tilstanden med grevens affærer blev ganske tydelig en måned efter hans død og overraskede alle med omfanget af gæld, som ingen havde anet. Gælden var dobbelt så stor som aktiverne.

Venner og slægtninge rådede Nikolaj til at frasige sig arven. Men han betragtede en sådan afvisning som en plet på sin fars minde, som han holdt helligt, og ville derfor ikke høre tale om at nægte og accepterede arven sammen med forpligtelsen til at betale gælden.

Så længe greven levede, havde hans sorgløse godmodighed øvet en ubestemmelig, men stærk magt over kreditorerne og holdt dem tilbage. Nu gjorde de alle på én gang deres krav gældende. Som altid i den slags tilfælde blev der kappestrid om, hvem der skulle have sine penge først, og de, der ligesom Mitenka havde fået deres gældsbreve forærende, var de mest ubønhørlige. Nikolaj fik hverken henstand eller fred. De samme mennesker, der syntes at have haft ondt af den gamle mand, som var skyld i deres tab – hvis det ellers var tab – forfulgte nu uden skånsel den unge arving, der frivilligt havde påtaget sig gælden og vitterlig ingen skyld havde i, at den var stiftet.

Ingen af de planer, Nikolaj prøvede, lykkedes; godset blev solgt på tvangsauktion for halvdelen af sin værdi, og halvdelen af gælden stod stadig ubetalt. Nikolaj tog imod de tredive tusind rubler, hans svoger Bezukhov (Pierre) tilbød ham, for at betale den gæld, han betragtede som ægte og skyldig for modtagne værdier. Og for at undgå fængsel for resten af gælden trådte han i statstjeneste.

Han kunne ikke vende tilbage til hæren, hvor han ville være blevet forfremmet til oberst ved næste ledige plads, for hans mor klamrede sig nu til ham som sit eneste hold i livet; og så trods sin modvilje mod at forblive i Moskva blandt folk, der havde kendt ham før, og trods sin afsky for statstjenesten, accepterede han en civil stilling i Moskva og lagde sin elskede uniform til side for at flytte ind i en lille lejlighed med sin mor og Sonja.

Natasja og Pierre boede i Petersborg på det tidspunkt og havde ingen klar forestilling om Nikolajs situation. Da han havde lånt penge af sin svoger, forsøgte Nikolaj at skjule sin elendige tilstand for ham. Hans stilling var desto vanskeligere, fordi han med sin løn på tolv hundrede rubler ikke blot skulle forsørge sig selv, men også sin mor og Sonja på en sådan måde, at hans mor ikke anede, at de var fattige. Grevinden kunne ikke fatte livet uden de luksusforhold, hun havde været vant til fra barnsben, og da hun ikke forstod, hvor svært det var for sin søn, krævede hun snart en vogn (som de ikke havde) for at sende efter en veninde, snart en dyr vin til sig selv, og snart penge til at købe en overraskelsesgave til Natasja eller Sonja, eller til Nikolaj selv.

Sonja holdt hus, passede sin tante, læste højt for hende, udholdt hendes luner og skjulte uvilje, og hjalp Nikolaj med at skjule deres fattigdom for den gamle grevinde. Nikolaj følte sig uhjælpeligt i gæld til Sonja for alt, hvad hun gjorde for hans mor, og beundrede hendes tålmodighed og hengivelse i høj grad, men forsøgte at holde sig på afstand af hende.

Han syntes i sit hjerte at bebrejde hende, at hun var for perfekt, og at der intet var at bebrejde hende. Hun havde alt det, folk værdsættes for, men lidt af det, der kunne have fået ham til at elske hende. Han følte, at jo mere han satte pris på hende, desto mindre elskede han hende. Han havde taget hende på ordet, da hun skrev ham sit frihedsbrev, og behandlede hende nu som om alt, hvad der var sket mellem dem, var glemt for længe siden og under ingen omstændigheder kunne gentage sig.

Nikolajs situation blev værre og værre. Tanken om at lægge noget til side af sin løn viste sig at være en drøm. Ikke blot sparede han intet, men for at opfylde sin mors krav stiftede han endda lidt gæld. Han kunne ikke se nogen udvej af denne situation. Tanken om at gifte sig med en rig kvinde, som hans kvindelige slægtninge foreslog, var ham imod. Den anden udvej — hans mors død — kom aldrig op i hans sind. Han ønskede intet og håbede intet og fandt dybt i hjertet en mørk og bitter glæde i at bære sine forhold med tålmod. Han forsøgte at undgå gamle bekendte med deres medlidenhed og påtrængende tilbud, undgik al underholdning og tidsfordriv, og selv i hjemmet foretog han sig intet ud over at lægge kabale med sin mor, vandre tavst rundt i stuen og ryge pibe efter pibe. Det var, som om han omhyggeligt værnede om den tungsindighed, der alene satte ham i stand til at holde sin stilling ud.

english.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: Natasha's marriage to Bezukhov, which took place in 1813, was the last happy event in the old Rostov family. Count Ilya Rostov died that same year, and—as always happens—with the father's death, the family fell apart.

The events of the previous year—the burning of Moscow and the flight from it, Prince Andrew's death, Natasha's despair, Petya's death, and the old countess's grief—fell blow after blow on the old count's head. He seemed unable to understand their meaning, and bowed his old head as if expecting and inviting more blows to finish him off. He appeared now frightened and bewildered, now unnaturally animated and energetic.

Natasha's wedding kept him busy for a while. He ordered dinners and suppers and obviously tried to appear cheerful, but his cheerfulness was no longer infectious as it had once been; on the contrary, it made those who knew and loved him feel sorry for him.

When Pierre and his wife had gone, the count grew very quiet and began complaining of depression. A few days later he fell ill and took to his bed. From the start, despite the doctor's reassurances, he knew he would never get up again. The countess spent two weeks in an armchair by his bed without undressing. Every time she gave him his medicine he sobbed quietly and kissed her hand. On his last day, weeping, he begged forgiveness from his wife, and also—though his absent son was not there—from his son Nicholas, for having squandered the family's fortune, which was the main thing he felt guilty about. After receiving communion and last rites, he died quietly, and the next day a crowd of acquaintances came to pay their final respects to the deceased. All those acquaintances who had so often dined and danced in his house, and who had so often mocked him behind his back, now said with a uniform feeling of inner self-reproach and tenderness: "Well, say what you like, he was a wonderful man. You don't find people like that anymore... And who doesn't have faults?"
It was precisely when the count's financial affairs had become so tangled that no one could say what would happen if he lived another year that he unexpectedly died.

Nicholas was with the Russian army in Paris when the news of his father's death reached him. He immediately resigned his commission and, without waiting for it to be accepted, took leave of absence and went to Moscow. Within a month of the count's death, the full scale of the financial chaos became clear, astonishing everyone with the enormous total of petty debts whose existence no one had suspected. The debts were twice the value of the estate.

Friends and relatives advised Nicholas to renounce the inheritance. But he considered such a refusal an insult to his father's memory, which he held sacred, and so he would not hear of refusing. He accepted the inheritance along with the obligation to pay the debts.

The creditors, who had been silent so long—restrained by the vague but powerful influence the count's careless good nature had exerted on them while he lived—now all rushed to press their claims at once. As always happens in such cases, a rivalry sprang up over whose claims would be paid first, and the very people who—like Mitenka and others—held promissory notes they had received as gifts now proved to be the most aggressive creditors. Nicholas was given no peace and no quarter. Those who had pitied the old man—the cause of their losses, if losses there really were—now fell mercilessly on his obviously innocent young son, who had voluntarily taken on the debts.

None of Nicholas's plans succeeded. The estate was sold at auction for half its value, and half the debts still remained unpaid. Nicholas accepted thirty thousand rubles from his brother-in-law Bezukhov to pay off the debts he considered genuinely binding—real debts to real people. And to avoid going to prison for the remainder, which he couldn't pay, he entered the civil service.

Returning to the army, where he would have been made colonel at the next vacancy, was out of the question, because his mother now clung to him as her only hold on life. And so despite his reluctance to stay in Moscow among people who had known him before, despite his distaste for the civil service, he took a minor government post, removed his beloved hussar uniform, and moved with his mother and Sonya into a small apartment on the Sivtsev Vrazhek.

Natasha and Pierre were living in Petersburg at the time and had no clear idea of Nicholas's situation. Having borrowed money from his brother-in-law, Nicholas tried to hide his wretched circumstances from him. His position was all the more difficult because, on his twelve-hundred-ruble salary, he had to support not only himself, his mother, and Sonya but had to shield his mother from their poverty. The countess could not imagine living without the luxuries she had known since childhood. Without understanding the difficulty, she kept demanding a carriage she no longer had to send for a friend, expensive delicacies for herself, and wine for her son.

Sonya kept house, waited on her aunt, read to her, endured her moods and secret resentment, and helped Nicholas hide their poverty from the old countess. Nicholas felt irredeemably indebted to Sonya for everything she was doing for his mother, and he admired her patience and devotion. But he tried to keep his distance from her.

He seemed in his heart to blame her for being too perfect, because there was nothing to blame her for. She had all the qualities people are valued for, but little that could have made him love her. He felt that the more he appreciated her, the less he loved her. He had taken her at her word when she wrote giving him his freedom, and now treated her as though everything between them had been long forgotten and could never, under any circumstances, be repeated.

Nicholas's financial situation kept getting worse and worse. The idea of saving something from his salary turned out to be a fantasy. Not only did he save nothing, but he even ran up small debts to meet his mother's demands. He could see no way out of his situation. The idea of marrying a rich woman, which his female relatives suggested, disgusted him. The only other way out—his mother's death—never entered his mind. He wished for nothing, hoped for nothing, and deep down took a dark, grim pleasure in stoically enduring his position. He tried to avoid old acquaintances with their expressions of pity and their offensive offers of help, avoided all entertainment and amusement, and even at home did nothing but play patience with his mother, pace silently around the room, and smoke pipe after pipe. He seemed determined to maintain within himself that gloomy state of mind in which alone he felt capable of bearing his situation.
